title: Does a bigger number always have a longer prime factorisation?
description: A claim about prime factorisations is tested with ninety six and one hundred and twenty one. Counting the primes in each shows the larger number has the shorter factorisation, which is a counterexample. Keeko's doubt, that one example is not enough, is answered with the meaning of a claim.
teaching_notes: One idea: a single counterexample is enough to disprove a claim. Watch for students who think a claim that works for some numbers must be true.

source: Anshu says: the larger a number is, the longer its prime fac
video_script.why: The child has seen many factorisations and now meets a claim that sounds sensible but can be tested.
video_script.substitution: Count the primes in each factorisation and compare the counts with the sizes of the numbers.
video_script.anchor: A claim written on the board, with the numbers ninety six and one hundred and twenty one to test it.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says one example is not enough, because the claim worked for other numbers. But a claim must hold for every number, so a single example where it fails is enough.

final_answer.value: The claim is false: 121 is larger than 96 but has a shorter factorisation
final_answer.spoken: the claim is false, since one hundred and twenty one is larger than ninety six but has a shorter factorisation

names.Ruhee: makes a claim about prime factorisations

maths_rules: 96 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 has six primes (32 x 3 = 96).
121 is larger than 96, but its factorisation is shorter, so the claim fails for this pair.
One such example, a counterexample, is enough to show the claim is false.
Slip: a claim that works for some numbers is not true unless it works for all.
video_script.design: One idea: a counterexample disproves a claim. Assumes prime factorisation. Wrong idea: one example is not enough. The claim stays on the board all video.
